about: Every paragraph the result page can show. `bands` holds one paragraph per god for each band that config/scoring.json marks `describe: true`; if a band has no paragraph the next weaker one is used. `neglected` is shown for the god opposite the lead. `tiers` opens the page; placeholders {lead}, {second}, {leadPole} and {secondPole} are filled in. The stories in the `strong` paragraphs come from the passages listed under `read` in gods.json.

tiers.clear: Your answers went furthest toward {lead}, and by a clear margin, so this is probably the god other people would name for you. {second} comes next. Read the first as what you do and the second as how you go about it.
tiers.clearAlone: {lead}, and nobody close behind. On the other six lines your answers stayed near the middle, so this one god accounts for most of what people notice about you.
tiers.shared: {lead} and {second}, with almost nothing between them. Both are yours. Which one turns up first probably depends on the room.
pantheios: Your answers stayed near the middle on all seven lines, so no god leads. There is a Greek word for that: pantheios, belonging to all the gods.

It is a result in its own right. You can take charge or hang back, plan or improvise, press the point or let it go, as the day requires, and you are seldom the most extreme person in the room about anything. People find you easy to work with and hard to sum up. You may have the same trouble.

Two things to check. If you chose the middle circle for most statements, take the test again and commit wherever a statement is even slightly more or less true of you than of the people you know. Then look at the leanings below, which show the gods you favour when you favour any.

zeus.lean: When nobody is deciding, you start to. You can leave it alone if someone else has it in hand, though you will have a view on how they are doing.
zeus.clear: You take the chair. Nobody asks you to and nobody seems to mind, because someone had to say what happens next and you already had. You hand out the jobs, and when it goes wrong you count that as yours too. What you cannot do for long is be led, or sit while a room talks its way to a decision you made ten minutes ago.
zeus.strong: In the Iliad Zeus offers to hang a gold chain from heaven and let every other god pull on it, to show that together they could not move him an inch. You have some of that. Things run through you, people come to you for the ruling, and you would rather carry the whole weight than share the say. Those under your roof are well protected. They are also seldom asked, and you tend to hear a second opinion as a challenge.

hades.lean: You say less than you know. A plan gets shared when it is finished, and you would sooner watch a room than work it.
hades.clear: Most of what you do happens where nobody is looking, and you prefer it that way. You keep your opinions until someone asks, finish the work before you mention it, and regard people who need an audience with mild suspicion. It protects what you are building. It also means that help, and credit, tend to arrive after you have stopped needing them.
hades.strong: What you think, what you want and what you are working on all stay below until you choose to bring them up, and applause does nothing for you. The Greeks avoided this god’s name and called him Plouton, the rich one, because everything of value was kept underground with him. People who love you can spend years outside the door. Meanwhile the decisions about you get made by whoever was willing to speak.

hermes.lean: Given a road you know and one you don’t, you take the second slightly more often than is sensible. New interests arrive easily. So far you still come home.
hermes.clear: You learn fast and get bored fast, in that order. You collect interests, introduce people who ought to have met, and can explain one world to another, which makes you useful at the start of nearly anything. The middle is harder. Routine costs you more than it costs other people, and there are a few half-built things behind you.
hermes.strong: Hermes was born in the morning, had invented the lyre by noon and stolen his brother’s cattle by evening, then lied about it so prettily that Zeus laughed. You are quick like that, and about as easy to hold. You would rather open five doors than furnish one room. It makes you inventive and very well connected. The same speed trades a promise for the next interesting thing, and now and then lets a clever answer do duty for a true one.

hestia.lean: You like your own chair. You would rather mend what works than replace it, and it takes a good reason to move you, though a good reason will.
hestia.clear: You have kept the same places, people and habits for years, and they have kept you. Others find you where they left you, which is rarer than it sounds and is why things tend to come back to your table. Change for its own sake looks like noise to you. Once in a while it was not noise, and you were the last to move.
hestia.strong: The fire, the routine and the people who come home to both matter more to you than anything new on offer, and several lives are steadier than they would be without yours in the middle. When the other gods ride out in procession, Plato says, Hestia alone stays in the house. Someone has to. The price is a world that stops at the doorstep, and chances that went by because taking them would have meant getting up.

apollo.lean: You like a plan and a clean finish. A loose end bothers you more than it bothers the person who left it.
apollo.clear: You plan, then do what the plan says, then check it, and people trust your work for exactly that reason. Work comes before play as a matter of course. A job left rough will sit in your mind until it is put right. Good enough is a phrase you understand and cannot quite feel.
apollo.strong: Two sayings were cut into his temple at Delphi: know yourself, and nothing in excess. You have taken the second one to excess. The discipline is real, and it has carried you further than talent carries most people. But the standard has started giving the orders. A flaw is hard to leave alone, rest has to be earned first, and the people near you sometimes feel marked.

dionysus.lean: You decide by feel a shade more than by plan, and you loosen quickly in good company. When something has to be finished you can still pull yourself together.
dionysus.clear: You go where the evening goes. When you love a thing you go into it completely, and a room is livelier once you are in it. You work in bursts, usually close to the deadline, usually well. Anything that needs the same small effort every day is in some danger from you.
dionysus.strong: You want to be taken over, by music, by company, by work that swallows the night, and you take people with you. Most of them are grateful. When Antony entered Ephesus the city hailed him as Dionysus, giver of joy, and Plutarch adds that to most people he turned out to be Dionysus the eater of raw flesh. It was the same god. Ask the ones who were counting on you the next morning.

aphrodite.lean: You hear how a remark will land before you make it, and you soften it. On small things you would sooner agree than argue.
aphrodite.clear: People relax around you and are not sure why. You read a room in a moment, say the thing that settles it, and tend to get your way because others end up wanting to give it to you. What suffers is the plain truth. You will let a point go to save the evening, and some of those points needed making.
aphrodite.strong: Aphrodite owned an embroidered band that held, Homer says, the kind of talk that steals the sense even from the wise. Hera borrowed it when she needed to get round Zeus. You seem to have been born wearing it. Almost anyone comes round to you in the end, and a quarrel rarely survives your walking in. The danger is that pleasing becomes the plan. You say what will be welcome, skip the fight you ought to have had, and can lose track of what you wanted yourself.

ares.lean: You say what you think a beat sooner than most, and you like a contest. If someone’s feelings are in the way you can still wait.
ares.clear: People know where they stand with you, since you have told them. You speak plainly, like to win, and walk toward the argument that everyone else is walking around. In a real fight you are who people want beside them. Not everything is one, though, and you have bruised a few who were never on the other side.
ares.strong: “You are the most hateful to me of all the gods on Olympus,” Zeus tells Ares in the Iliad, “for strife is always dear to you.” Then he has him healed, because Ares is his son and there will be other wars. You are brave, you are honest, and when something needs confronting you are already on your feet. You also escalate when pushed, compete over things that do not matter, and have won arguments that cost more than they were worth.

athena.lean: Pressure gets to you later than it gets to other people, and you tend to think before you answer. A bad enough day still lands.
athena.clear: When it goes wrong your voice stays level. You sleep on decisions, have forgotten an insult by the weekend, and see other people’s problems clearly enough that they keep bringing them to you. The calm is real. From outside it can look like not caring, and you do sometimes underrate how hard a thing is for someone who feels it more than you do.
athena.strong: When Achilles has his sword half out to kill Agamemnon, it is Athena who takes him by the hair and tells him to put it back, and that he will be paid three times over later. She is right, and he obeys. Under pressure you get cooler and more exact, you are several moves ahead, and a setback leaves hardly a mark. You are who people want in a crisis. Afterwards is harder. Feelings get managed that ought to be felt, and those who are less steady start to look, to you, merely weak.

poseidon.lean: Things reach you faster and stay longer than they do with most people, and it shows on your face. You come back to level fairly soon.
poseidon.clear: Nobody has to guess how you are. You feel things at full size, your mood sets the weather for the day, and you often know something is wrong in a room before anyone has said it. People find you vivid and warm. They have also learned to check the sky. A slight can stay with you long after the other person has forgotten making it.
poseidon.strong: Poseidon lost Athens to Athena in a fair contest and flooded the plain anyway. With you, too, everything arrives at full strength, joy as much as anger, and it moves whoever is standing near. Most of your power to care about things comes from there. So do the decisions made mid-storm, the grudges that outlive their cause, and the way the people around you have learned to brace.

hera.lean: Your people and your promises tend to outweigh your own plans. You like knowing where you belong, and you keep a corner for yourself.
hera.clear: You say “we” and mean it. You keep your word, remember the dates, and take your family’s side, or your firm’s, in front of outsiders whatever you say to them in private. People can build on you. It leaves you open, of course. You can be let down badly, and little hurts you more than disloyalty.
hera.strong: At Stymphalus, Pausanias says, Hera had three sanctuaries: as girl, as wife, and as the one left alone. A whole life counted in its ties, and yours is counted the same way. You commit completely, stay through the bad years, and things last because you do not leave. Few people are as dependable. The same grip does not loosen easily. You watch for betrayal, you remember it, and letting someone go their own way is hard for you even when it is right.

artemis.lean: You need a bit more time on your own terms than most people do, and you read the small print before you join anything. Close ties still matter to you.
artemis.clear: You keep your own ground and your own rules. A few days alone put you right, and you steer clear of any arrangement that would leave you owing or answering to someone. You are self-reliant, clear about your limits, and quick to step in for anyone who cannot defend themselves. People who want more of you than that tend to find the door half open, which is as open as it goes.
artemis.strong: As a small child on her father’s knee, Callimachus says, Artemis asked for a bow, the mountains, and never to be married. Zeus laughed and gave her all of it. You belong to yourself in the same way. Solitude restores you, obligation chafes, and you would sooner go without than be managed or claimed. It gives you focus and an integrity that is hard to buy. You also leave before anyone can ask you to stay, punish a crossed line harder than it deserved, and end up more alone than you intended.

demeter.lean: You notice before most people do when someone needs something, and you do something about it. You can also leave people to manage.
demeter.clear: You know who has not eaten. You know who is struggling and who is ready for more, and you act on it without being asked. Feeding, teaching and bringing people on is the work you like best, and they do grow around you. Your own needs come last, by a distance. And it is hard for you, harder than you let on, when someone you raised stops needing you.
demeter.strong: When her daughter was taken, Demeter stopped the grain. Nothing grew for a year, and the gods themselves went without offerings until Persephone was given back. That is the scale of it. Other people’s needs and growth arrange your days, and you give time, food and attention without counting, to more people than know it. The year without grain is yours as well: the help nobody asked for, the holding on, and the hollow when the ones you tended move on.

hephaestus.lean: A problem you can get your hands on holds you better than small talk does. You like people well enough, in the right dose.
hephaestus.clear: You build, repair and improve, and can lose an afternoon inside an object or a system without noticing it go. You show that you care by making a thing work for someone. Your work holds up because you stay with it. The people can feel second to the project, and what the work was meant to say for you sometimes never gets said.
hephaestus.strong: When Thetis comes to ask for armour she finds Hephaestus at the bellows, sweating, with twenty tripods half made and gold wheels fitted under them so that they can roll to the feast on their own. Left alone with a hard problem and good tools you are as happy as that, and what you make is exact and built to last. The workshop is also a very good place to hide. You answer a feeling with a fix, let friendships thin while you perfect something, and can turn bitter when nobody notices the craft.

neglected.zeus: Zeus is owed something by anyone who keeps as quiet as you do. It need not be much. Say what you think before you are asked. Take the decision that is plainly yours. Show the work while it can still be of use to someone.
neglected.hades: You have left Hades almost nothing, which is the usual way with people who run things. He would settle for a little restraint. Let someone else decide one matter and live with what they choose. Keep a plan to yourself until it is ready. Spend an hour somewhere nobody is waiting on your word.
neglected.hermes: Hermes gets short measure from you. One new thing at a time would do: a road you have not walked, a person from outside your circle, a way of doing something that you did not grow up with.
neglected.hestia: Hestia has seen very little of you. What she asks is that you stay. Finish one thing before the next is begun. Keep one small habit for a whole year. Go back to a place, or a person, at the point where you would usually move on.
neglected.apollo: Apollo is the one going without. He wants a plan that is kept after the mood has gone: one timetable, one standard held, one piece of work finished early and not rescued late.
neglected.dionysus: Dionysus is owed an evening. Time with no purpose and no score would cover it: music, a long table, something you are bad at and enjoy anyway. Pentheus refused him outright, and Euripides wrote a play about what happened next.
neglected.aphrodite: Aphrodite gets little from you. Her due is that you make it easy for the other person once in a while. Ask before you argue. Give away the small point. Say the hard thing in a form that can be heard.
neglected.ares: Ares has had nothing from you in a while. One honest disagreement would settle the account. Say the unwelcome thing plainly, let the evening suffer for it, and notice that the friendship is still there in the morning.
neglected.athena: Athena is waiting, which she is good at. Her due is the pause: a night’s sleep before you reply, a moment spent asking what you want to happen next, a plan made while the water is flat.
neglected.poseidon: Poseidon goes unpaid. He asks that you let a thing land before you solve it. Admit that it hurt, or that it mattered. Let one person see you unsettled.
neglected.hera: Hera has no claim on you yet, and that is what she minds. Her due is a promise that binds. Let somebody count on you. Stay through a dull stretch. Accept the kind of help that leaves you in someone’s debt.
neglected.artemis: Artemis has been crowded out. She wants ground that is yours alone: a day that answers to no one, a pursuit that serves neither the family nor the firm, and enough trust to let people go off and come back.
neglected.demeter: Demeter is owed your attention, with nothing in it to fix. Ask someone how they are and stay for the answer. Teach what you know. Eat with the others.
neglected.hephaestus: Hephaestus gets what is left over, which is nothing. His due is work that belongs only to you: a craft, a problem, an object you can lose an afternoon in while nobody needs you for anything.

method: The test is short: {count} statements, {perGod} to a god. Nobody has yet tried it on a large group of people, so the lines it draws between a lean, a clear pull and a strong one are guesses. Take the result as a sketch.

Each pair is scored as one god minus the other, so someone strong on both sides lands in the middle. It happens most with people and things, since plenty of us tend and make. If the result surprises you, ask two people who know you well, and believe them over this page.
